newsitem.title: USA: Detroit upgrades could open door to more investors.
newsitem.headline: Detroit upgrades could open door to more investors.

text.p: A heaping helping of good ratings news for Detroit over the last week may help nudge more buyers to invest in the Motor City's debt, municipal market participants said Friday.
"I think it improves the bid a bit and the marketability of (Detroit's) bonds," said William VanderWheele, a managing member of Roney & Co in Detroit.
A sales representative in Detroit said his clients holding Detroit paper were pleased with the rating news, adding "they might add to their positions because of the upgrades."

A steady rain of rating improvements started on October 17, when Moody's Investors Service restored an investment grade rating of Baa to nearly $300 million of Detroit's outstanding unlimited tax general obligation debt. The city's rating with Moody's had stood at Ba1 since July 1992.

On Tuesday, Standard & Poor's Corp, which maintains a BBB rating on Detroit's unlimited tax GO debt and a BBB-minus rating on the city's limited tax GO debt, revised its rating outlook to positive from stable.
The agency pointed out that it expects to upgrade Detroit's long-term rating "as the city's financial position rebounds from past weaknesses."
Fitch Investors Service weighed in on Thursday by upgrading to BBB from BBB-minus its rating on Detroit's unlimited and limited tax GO bonds.
A Chicago-based underwriter said the restoration of Detroit's investment grade rating from Moody's would open up the market to "a lot more buyers."
James Schmidt, president of Schmidt Securities Inc in Bloomington Hills, Mich., said secondary market activity in Detroit debt had improved even before the upgrades were announced.
"The perception of Detroit had changed before the rating changes took place," he said, adding there was a scarcity of the city's paper in the market.

Still another trader said that despite the upgrades, interest in Detroit paper was limited to "a few high-yield players." The trader said he doubted retail investors would be interested in the city's bonds given lingering concerns about the viability of Detroit's tax base outside of its downtown.
Many municipal market participants gave Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer much of the credit for the city's financial turnaround in the eyes of the rating agencies.
"This is a good sign for what Mayor Archer has done in the rebound of the city," VanderWheele said.

Richard Ciccarone, a senior vice president at Van Kampen American Capital in Oakbrook Terrace, Ill., said Detroit's positive momentum became apparent after General Motors Corp announced earlier this year it was moving its corporate headquarters to the Renaissance Center.
"It seems to me the market saw a bullish signal on the rebuilding of the heart of the city's downtown," he said.

Other positive signs cited by ratings agencies were plans to build new professional sports stadiums in the city's downtown, investment spurred by Detroit's federal empowerment zone status, Chrysler's construction of a new engine plant, conservative budgeting practices and growing taxable property valuation.
Still rating analysts warned the Motor City owes much of its improved economic performance to automotive-related manufacturing, which is cyclical in nature.
In its rating release, Fitch said Detroit's ability "to sustain economically sensitive revenues in the face of future economic cycles will continue to be a risk."
Other risk factors include the city's high debt burden and vulnerability of certain revenues, including state revenue sharing.
--Karen Pierog, 312-408-8647
